messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Vignette:
At 72, Minh Tran came to treatment at his wife’s urging after months of becoming “too jumpy to live with,” as he put it with visible embarrassment. Minh is a Vietnamese American man who has spent the last several years working as a nanny for a family with two young children. He described the traumatic event as physical abuse by a romantic partner several decades earlier, during a relationship he had rarely spoken about in any detail. When he finally did describe it, he returned to one night in particular. He had been in a dark bedroom after an argument, trying to keep quiet and not provoke anything further, when his partner came at him suddenly. Minh remembered the sense of being trapped in the dark, the shock of movement appearing beside him before he could orient himself, and his body folding into a protective position on the bed and then against the wall as he braced for more blows. Even now, when he tried to tell it, the fear arrived in him all at once. He did not speak of it as a past event recalled from a distance; he spoke as if the terror were waiting just under the surface, unchanged.

In the years after the abuse, Minh built his life around staying calm, keeping things smooth, and never letting anger show. He had come to believe that allowing himself to feel anger at all was dangerous, so he tried to press it down immediately, even in minor daily frustrations. If a driver cut him off, if a parent he worked for came home late without notice, if one of the children hit or yelled at him in a childish tantrum, he would smile tightly, say he was fine, and move on. He described this almost as a rule for survival: never add heat to a situation, never let himself become someone who could fight back or be fought with. Alongside that, he narrowed his life in quieter ways. He avoided being in the dark whenever he could. At home he kept lights on in the hallway and bathroom at night. If his wife suggested a movie in a dim theater, he found a reason not to go. He also began avoiding anything he thought might be stressful, turning down invitations, stepping back from errands at busy times, and arranging his days to be as predictable as possible.

His work as a nanny brought him into contact with reminders he could not always control. The children he cared for often darted into rooms, ran up behind him, or reached suddenly for his arm while playing. When a small body moved unexpectedly near him, Minh reacted as if danger were already there; he would flinch hard, pull away, or turn abruptly with his heart pounding before he could register that it was only a child. Loudness was not what got him most. It was sudden movement in his peripheral vision, someone appearing beside him without warning, that seemed to seize his whole body. He remained tense even in the family’s bright, orderly home, telling himself he knew he was safe while noticing that his shoulders stayed raised and his breathing shallow. He could sit in a quiet room during the children’s nap and still feel unable to relax.

When memories of the abuse surfaced, Minh found them deeply disorienting. He sometimes said the memory felt as if it belonged to another man, not to him, as though he were describing something that happened to a stranger whose life brushed uncomfortably close to his own. But that distance could vanish instantly. If the memory came back, the original terror returned with it, vivid and immediate. He noticed that his body would draw in on itself without his meaning to: arms close, torso tight, neck bent, as though he were once again trying to protect himself from another strike in the dark. Those moments frightened him not only because of what he remembered, but because his body seemed to know the position before he had words for it.

Over time these habits affected his marriage and his work. His wife grew frustrated with the lights left on and with his refusal to go places that felt even mildly stressful. At work he became increasingly preoccupied with preventing surprises, asking the children to announce themselves, keeping doors open, and positioning himself so no one could approach from behind. What finally brought him in was an incident in the family’s kitchen when one of the children ran up and grabbed his waist from the side. Minh lurched away so abruptly that the child started crying, and he was left shaken and ashamed. He worried that he could no longer trust his own reactions, even in a house he knew well. Sitting in the clinic, he said he wanted help because he was tired of living as if danger could step out from any dim corner or sudden movement. What frightened him most was the sense that the old terror could still take hold of his body so completely; what he hoped for, cautiously, was to feel present in his own life instead of braced against it.
